issues.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance of a sale agreement requires proof of a concluded, valid and enforceable contract, and the discretionary remedy must be granted according to judicial principles after considering the evidence and circumstances.
material_facts: The claim for specific performance rested on a written sale agreement that referred to an earlier agreement, but the earlier agreement was neither produced nor exhibited.
The trial court found that the later agreement and payment of consideration had not been proved; the High Court reversed that finding and granted specific performance.
The High Court relied in part on a criminal court’s observations about the agreement, while not considering documents from earlier proceedings that bore on the claim concerning possession.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not properly considered the evidence and circumstances relevant to whether the alleged agreement was proved and whether specific performance was appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s decree for specific performance was set aside, the trial court’s judgment was restored, and the suit was liable to be dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, specific performance is discretionary and the discretion must be exercised on sound and reasonable judicial principles, not arbitrarily. A plaintiff must establish a valid and enforceable contract, including consensus ad idem on the vital and fundamental terms of sale; a court will not make a contract for the parties. The plaintiff must also establish continued readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part. An oral agreement may be enforceable, but the party seeking specific performance bears a heavy burden to prove a concluded agreement. The Court applied Koillipara Sriramulu v. T. Aswatha Narayana on oral agreements; Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey on the statutory discretion; Mayawanti v. Kaushalya Devi on the need for a valid and enforceable contract; and K. Prakash v. B.R. Sampath Kumar and Zarina Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam on the exercise of discretion and the requirements for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and alleged_sale_agreement_referred_to_an_earlier_agreement and earlier_agreement_not_produced and criminal_findings_relied_on_for_execution and independent_civil_assessment_of_evidence_inadequate

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.alleged_sale_agreement_referred_to_an_ea: The written agreement relied on by the plaintiff referred to an earlier agreement as part of the claimed transaction.
predicates.earlier_agreement_not_produced: The plaintiff did not produce or exhibit the earlier agreement referred to in the written agreement.
predicates.criminal_findings_relied_on_for_executio: The court granting specific performance relied on observations or findings from a criminal proceeding concerning execution of the agreement.
predicates.independent_civil_assessment_of_evidence: The civil court granting specific performance did not adequately assess the evidence and circumstances independently, including material records bearing on the claim.

issues.definition: When a suit seeks specific performance and the alleged contract depends on an unproduced earlier agreement and criminal findings without an adequate independent civil assessment, the remedy is denied.

issues.legal_issue: Findings or evidence in a criminal proceeding cannot, without an independent finding by the civil court, conclusively establish the existence of an agreement for specific performance.
material_facts: The same written agreement was considered in a criminal proceeding and observations about its execution were recorded there.
The High Court treated those observations as supporting proof of execution in the civil suit for specific performance.
The Supreme Court held that the criminal court’s evidence and findings could not conclusively prove the existence of the agreement in the civil suit without an independent civil finding.
issues.conclusion: The criminal court’s findings could not be treated as conclusive proof of the agreement’s existence for granting specific performance without an independent finding by the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act was invoked in the High Court’s treatment of the criminal court’s observations. The Supreme Court held that evidence and findings recorded by criminal courts cannot be conclusive proof of a fact, particularly the existence of an agreement relied on to obtain specific performance, in the absence of an independent finding by the civil court. The criminal proceeding’s findings therefore do not replace the civil court’s own assessment of the evidence.

predicates.civil_specific_performance_proceeding: A civil proceeding seeks specific performance of an alleged agreement.
predicates.criminal_court_findings_about_agreement_: A party or court relies on findings or evidence from a criminal proceeding concerning the alleged agreement.
predicates.independent_civil_finding_on_agreement_a: The civil court has not independently found, on its own assessment of the evidence, that the agreement exists.

issues.definition: When a civil specific-performance proceeding relies on criminal court findings about an agreement without an independent civil finding, those criminal findings do not conclusively prove the agreement.
